findings.evidence:
The Stripe client is deleted and replaced by the Paylane client in the same
release. There is no switch between the two: keeping both would double the
code to maintain. The Stripe account is closed the day after the release.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: All traffic moves at deploy
findings.recommendation: Keep a way back until Paylane is proven in production: keep the Stripe client behind a configuration switch (or a gradual rollout) for a defined period, and keep the Stripe account open until that period ends. Failure scenario: Paylane has an outage, rejects valid cards or a defect appears in the new client a few days after the release; redeploying the previous version brings back the Stripe client, but the Stripe account is already closed, so card payments stop entirely with no rollback, and the next release is up to a week away. State the rollback procedure and the date the Stripe account may be closed in the design.
findings.title: The switch to Paylane has no way back

findings.evidence:
A new worker, `settlement-worker`, runs at 02:00, fetches the day's Paylane
payments and matches them to orders. It runs as a Kubernetes CronJob and
writes its result to the database.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: A worker settles payments nightly
findings.recommendation: Decide how an operator learns that a run failed or did not run: a log at start and end with the run's counts, a metric or last-success timestamp, and an alert when the CronJob fails or no successful run is recorded for the day. Failure scenario: the Paylane API is unreachable at 02:00 or the job crashes; the CronJob fails, nothing is written and, since the only alert planned (spec "A payment without order") fires from a successful run, finance is never told that the day's payments were not settled. Add a scenario for a failed run to the spec and a task for it.
findings.title: The settlement worker can fail without anyone seeing it
